kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world.problem: Opening SharedPreferences with MODE_WORLD_READABLE makes the file readable by every other app installed on the device. This mode is deprecated for that reason but still appears in older code.
kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world.impact: Any malicious app can read your saved data — settings, IDs, even credentials if you stored them here.
kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world.fix: Use Context.MODE_PRIVATE. For sensitive values, use EncryptedSharedPreferences from androidx.security:security-crypto.

kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world-writable.problem: MODE_WORLD_WRITABLE lets any other app on the device modify your preference file. It is deprecated but still found in legacy apps.
kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world-writable.impact: A malicious app can corrupt your data, change app behavior, or escalate privileges if your code trusts these values.
kotlin-shared-prefs-mode-world-writable.fix: Use Context.MODE_PRIVATE. If you need cross-app data, use a properly secured ContentProvider with permissions.

kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-password.problem: You are storing a password as a plaintext string in SharedPreferences. The underlying XML file lives in the app sandbox but is trivially readable on a rooted device or from a backup.
kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-password.impact: Credentials leak as soon as the device is backed up, rooted, or examined by malware that targets your package.
kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-password.fix: Use androidx.security.crypto.EncryptedSharedPreferences, or store an Android Keystore-backed token instead of a raw password.

kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-token.problem: Auth tokens stored in plain SharedPreferences are readable by anyone with access to the app's data directory (root, backups, forensic tools).
kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-token.impact: Stolen tokens give an attacker the user's session on your backend until the token expires or is revoked.
kotlin-shared-prefs-plaintext-token.fix: Use EncryptedSharedPreferences, or store the token encrypted with a key kept in the Android Keystore.

kotlin-webview-js-enabled.problem: Enabling JavaScript on a WebView lets remote pages run scripts inside your app's WebView context. Combined with addJavascriptInterface or file access, this can become an attack surface.
kotlin-webview-js-enabled.impact: Compromised or attacker-controlled pages can call exposed JS interfaces, exfiltrate session data, or pivot into native code.
kotlin-webview-js-enabled.fix: Only enable JS when you control the loaded content. Never load untrusted URLs in a JS-enabled WebView, and avoid addJavascriptInterface on Android < 17.

kotlin-webview-file-access.problem: allowFileAccess = true lets the WebView load file:// URLs. If you also load remote content or accept user-supplied URLs, the page can navigate into local files.
kotlin-webview-file-access.impact: An attacker can read arbitrary files inside your app sandbox by chaining a malicious URL.
kotlin-webview-file-access.fix: Set allowFileAccess = false (the default since API 30) and serve local assets via WebViewAssetLoader instead.

kotlin-webview-universal-access.problem: allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs lets a file:// page make XHR/fetch requests to any origin, bypassing the same-origin policy entirely.
kotlin-webview-universal-access.impact: If any local HTML file is reachable by an attacker (downloads, exports), it can steal data from any web origin the user is logged into.
kotlin-webview-universal-access.fix: Leave this setting at its default (false). Never enable it on a WebView that loads untrusted content.

kotlin-http-cleartext.problem: A cleartext http:// URL appears in the source. Traffic to this endpoint is unencrypted and visible on the network path.
kotlin-http-cleartext.impact: Attackers on the same Wi-Fi or upstream network can read and modify the data — credentials, tokens, API responses.
kotlin-http-cleartext.fix: Use https:// and configure Network Security Config to forbid cleartext (cleartextTrafficPermitted="false").

kotlin-hardcoded-api-key.problem: An API key is declared as a const val directly in the source. The APK is just a zip — anyone can decompile it and read the constant.
kotlin-hardcoded-api-key.impact: Anyone can extract the key, call your APIs on your account, exhaust quotas, or run up your bill.
kotlin-hardcoded-api-key.fix: Move the key out of source: read it from a gitignored local.properties via BuildConfig, fetch from a backend, or proxy the API call server-side.

kotlin-hardcoded-secret.problem: A SECRET constant is embedded in source. Decompiling the APK reveals it instantly — obfuscation does not hide string literals from a determined attacker.
kotlin-hardcoded-secret.impact: Signing keys, encryption keys, or shared secrets leak to anyone who downloads the app.
kotlin-hardcoded-secret.fix: Never ship secrets in the APK. Use BuildConfig for build-time values that are not actually secret, and a backend or Android Keystore for real secrets.

kotlin-runtime-exec.problem: Runtime.getRuntime().exec runs a shell command. If any part of the command string comes from user input, an attacker can inject extra commands.
kotlin-runtime-exec.impact: Arbitrary command execution inside your app's sandbox — file reads, network calls, abuse of granted permissions.
kotlin-runtime-exec.fix: Avoid shell exec on Android. If you genuinely need a subprocess, pass an array of arguments and never interpolate user-controlled values.

kotlin-weak-crypto-md5.problem: MD5 is cryptographically broken: collisions are cheap to compute. It is unsafe for signatures, password hashing, or integrity checks.
kotlin-weak-crypto-md5.impact: An attacker can forge data that hashes to the same value, bypassing integrity or authentication checks built on MD5.
kotlin-weak-crypto-md5.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger for general hashing. For password hashing, use BCrypt, Scrypt, or Argon2 — never a raw hash.

kotlin-weak-crypto-sha1.problem: SHA-1 is deprecated by NIST and broken in practice — collision attacks have been demonstrated. It is unsafe for new signatures or integrity checks.
kotlin-weak-crypto-sha1.impact: Attackers can craft collisions to bypass signature checks or impersonate legitimate data.
kotlin-weak-crypto-sha1.fix: Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for hashing, and HMAC-SHA256 for message authentication.

kotlin-pending-intent-flag-mutable.problem: A PendingIntent created with FLAG_MUTABLE can be modified by the system component that receives it. On Android 12+, mutability is required to be explicit because of past abuse.
kotlin-pending-intent-flag-mutable.impact: Other apps or system components can alter the Intent to redirect it, change its extras, or fire it against unintended targets.
kotlin-pending-intent-flag-mutable.fix: Use FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless you specifically need a mutable PendingIntent (e.g. inline reply). Combine with FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT as needed.

kotlin-log-sensitive.problem: Log.d (or similar) prints a message that mentions password, token, or secret. Android logs are readable by adb and end up in crash reports, vendor diagnostics, and bug-report dumps.
kotlin-log-sensitive.impact: Sensitive values leak to anyone who can pull logs — including support tools and shared crash-report services.
kotlin-log-sensitive.fix: Never log credentials or tokens. If you need to log presence, log only a fixed marker ("token present") or a non-reversible hash prefix.

kotlin-trust-all-hostname.problem: A HostnameVerifier that always returns true tells TLS not to check whether the server certificate matches the URL hostname.
kotlin-trust-all-hostname.impact: Anyone able to present any valid certificate can impersonate your backend — full man-in-the-middle, credential and data theft.
kotlin-trust-all-hostname.fix: Remove the custom verifier. If you need a custom CA, configure Network Security Config; for pinning, use OkHttp CertificatePinner.

kotlin-double-bang.problem: The !! operator forces a nullable value to non-null and throws NullPointerException at runtime if the value is null.
kotlin-double-bang.impact: Crashes in production whenever the value is unexpectedly null — defeats Kotlin's null safety guarantees.
kotlin-double-bang.fix: Use ?.let { ... }, requireNotNull(x) { "reason" } with a clear message, or an explicit null check with a fallback path.

kotlin-empty-catch.problem: The catch block is empty — exceptions are caught and silently discarded.
kotlin-empty-catch.impact: Real bugs become invisible. Network failures, IO errors, and security exceptions all disappear without a trace, making the app harder to debug and easier to misuse.
kotlin-empty-catch.fix: At minimum, log the exception (Log.w(TAG, "...", e)). Better: handle the specific exception types you expect and let the rest propagate.

kotlin-runblocking-on-main.problem: runBlocking blocks the calling thread until the coroutine finishes. If called on the main thread, the UI freezes; long blocks trigger an ANR (Application Not Responding) dialog.
kotlin-runblocking-on-main.impact: Janky UI, ANR crashes, and bad app-store reviews. Background work that should be async becomes a hard stall.
kotlin-runblocking-on-main.fix: Launch a coroutine in the appropriate scope (lifecycleScope, viewModelScope) with the right dispatcher (Dispatchers.IO/Default) instead of runBlocking.

kotlin-println-prod.problem: println writes to System.out, which on Android ends up in logcat but cannot be filtered by tag or stripped from release builds easily.
kotlin-println-prod.impact: Noisy logs in production, no way to gate by log level, and possible leaks of debug data in released APKs.
kotlin-println-prod.fix: Use Timber (Timber.d("...")) or android.util.Log with a tag. Configure ProGuard/R8 to strip Log calls from release builds.

kotlin-todo-fn-call.problem: Kotlin's built-in TODO() function throws NotImplementedError when executed. Leaving it in a code path that ships means a guaranteed crash for any user who hits it.
kotlin-todo-fn-call.impact: Hard crash for end users — and unlike a comment, the compiler does not warn you it is still there.
kotlin-todo-fn-call.fix: Implement the missing branch, or replace TODO() with an explicit error that you intend to ship (and gate it behind a feature flag if needed).

kotlin-intent-getextra-no-check.problem: intent.getStringExtra returns data supplied by another app or component — it is fully untrusted external input. Using it without null and validity checks invites bugs and abuse.
kotlin-intent-getextra-no-check.impact: NullPointerExceptions, malformed-input crashes, and in some cases security bugs (path traversal, deep-link injection) if the value is used to build URLs or file paths.
kotlin-intent-getextra-no-check.fix: Always check for null, validate length and format, and constrain to an allowlist where possible. Treat extras like any other untrusted input.
